P.w: Encyclopedic art museum on Museum Mile with over 1.5 million works spanning 5,000 years, from Egyptian temples to European masters.
P.k: Pay-what-you-wish only for NY State residents; others pay a fixed admission. Closed Wednesdays.

P.w: 843-acre landscaped park by Olmsted and Vaux running from 59th to 110th Street, with Bethesda Terrace, the Ramble, and the Reservoir loop.
1931 Art Deco skyscraper with 86th and 102nd floor observatories offering 360-degree views across the city and beyond.
P.k: Timed tickets recommended; sunset slots sell out. Open late, past 11pm.

P.w: Open-air observation deck atop Rockefeller Center with an unobstructed head-on view of the Empire State Building and Central Park.
P.k: Entrance is on West 50th Street between Fifth and Sixth Avenues.

P.ad: Gansevoort Street & Washington Street, New York, NY 10014
P.w: 1.45-mile elevated park built on a former freight rail viaduct, running through Chelsea past gardens, art installations, and city views.
P.k: Southern entrance at Gansevoort St has elevator access. Free.

P.w: 1913 Beaux-Arts rail terminal with a celestial-mural ceiling over the Main Concourse and the acoustic Whispering Gallery by the Oyster Bar ramp.
P.k: Stand in opposite corners of the tiled archway to hear a whisper across the vault.

P.n: New York Public Library, Stephen A. Schwarzman Building
P.w: 1911 Beaux-Arts main branch guarded by the marble lions Patience and Fortitude, home to the vast third-floor Rose Main Reading Room.
P.k: Free entry; Rose Reading Room open Monday to Saturday.

P.ad: 99 Margaret Corbin Drive, New York, NY 10040
P.w: The Met's branch for medieval European art in Fort Tryon Park, built from parts of five French cloisters and home to the Unicorn Tapestries.
P.k: Far uptown in Washington Heights; admission is included with a Met ticket.

P.w: Greenwich Village square anchored by the Washington Arch and a central fountain, a longtime hub for street performers, chess, and NYU life.
P.k: Free; liveliest on warm weekend afternoons.

P.w: Henry Clay Frick's Gilded Age mansion showing Old Master paintings by Vermeer, Rembrandt, and Bellini; reopened April 2025 after a major renovation.
P.k: The mansion's second floor is now open to the public for the first time.

P.w: J.P. Morgan's 1906 private library in Murray Hill, with a three-tier tapestry-hung study and holdings from Gutenberg Bibles to literary manuscripts.
P.k: Closed Mondays; the historic library rooms are the highlight.

P.w: Restored 19th-century tenement telling immigrant stories through recreated apartments; entry is only by guided tour from the visitor center.
P.k: Tours must be booked; the museum interior is not open for free walk-ins.

P.w: Hidden one-acre park perched 40 feet above the Financial District, with a lawn, boardwalk, and East River views over the Brooklyn Bridge.
P.k: Reach it via an easy-to-miss escalator set back from Water Street.

P.w: Free Washington Heights museum with the finest collection of Spanish art outside Spain, including Goya, El Greco, and Sorolla's Vision of Spain murals.
P.k: Free timed ticket required as of January 2026.

P.ad: 555 Edgecombe Avenue, Apt 3F, New York, NY 10032
P.w: Free living-room jazz concert held every Sunday since 1993 in a Sugar Hill apartment, run by pianist Marjorie Eliot and family.
P.k: Sundays at 3pm; doors around 2:30pm. Free, donations welcome; arrive early for a seat.

P.ad: City Hall Station, New York, NY 10007
P.w: Ornate 1904 station with Guastavino-tiled vaults and skylights, closed to service since 1945; NY Transit Museum runs occasional member tours.
P.k: No regular access; you can glimpse it by staying on a downtown 6 train past the Brooklyn Bridge stop as it loops.

P.w: 52-acre garden famed for its Japanese Hill-and-Pond Garden and springtime cherry-blossom esplanade.
Encyclopedic art museum on Eastern Parkway with Egyptian holdings and Judy Chicago's The Dinner Party.
526-acre Olmsted and Vaux park with the Long Meadow, a lake, and the Prospect Park Zoo.
Seaside amusement park home to the 1927 wooden Cyclone coaster; reopened for the 2026 season March 30.
478-acre 1838 garden cemetery and National Historic Landmark with monuments, ponds, and skyline views.
Restored 1922 carousel in a glass pavilion in Brooklyn Bridge Park beneath the Brooklyn Bridge.

P.ad: Washington St at Water St, Brooklyn, NY 11201
P.w: Cobblestoned Washington Street framing the Manhattan Bridge tower, one of NYC's most photographed views.
Cantilevered esplanade over the BQE with panoramic views of Lower Manhattan and the harbor.
Museum inside a decommissioned 1936 subway station with vintage subway cars on original track.
Family park built around the 1920 Wonder Wheel, a 150-foot NYC-landmark Ferris wheel with swinging cars.
1892 triumphal arch honoring Civil War veterans, anchoring Grand Army Plaza at Prospect Park's entrance.
Tiny Williamsburg community museum of NYC ephemera behind a bodega-style canopy; open Thursday-Sunday.
Five-acre Williamsburg waterfront park on the former Domino Sugar Refinery site with salvaged syrup tanks.
Open-air street-art gallery of rotating murals across warehouse walls around Troutman St and St. Nicholas Ave.
Historic-house museum of Weeksville, a free Black community founded in 1838, with restored Hunterfly Road Houses.

P.ad: New York City Building, Flushing Meadows Corona Park, Corona, NY 11368
P.w: Home of the Panorama of the City of New York, a 9,335 sq ft scale model of all five boroughs built for the 1964 World's Fair, with 895,000 buildings.

P.ad: Flushing Meadows Corona Park, Corona, NY 11368
P.w: The 140-foot stainless-steel globe built for the 1964 World's Fair, ringed by fountains and the borough's most iconic landmark.
Isamu Noguchi's own museum of stone, metal and wood sculpture arranged around a serene indoor-outdoor garden he designed himself.

P.ad: 90-16 Rockaway Beach Blvd, Rockaway Beach, NY 11693
P.w: A 5.5-mile boardwalk on the Atlantic and NYC's only legal surfing beach, with designated surf zones and taco stands along the sand.

P.ad: 22-25 Jackson Ave, Long Island City, NY 11101
P.w: Contemporary art in a converted 1890s public school, MoMA's edgier affiliate, now free admission with rotating experimental installations.
The modest Corona home where Louis and Lucille Armstrong lived from 1943, preserved with his den intact; guided 40-minute tours only.

P.ad: 32-01 Vernon Blvd, Long Island City, NY 11106
P.w: A former illegal dumpsite turned free waterfront sculpture park on the East River, with rotating large-scale outdoor commissions and Manhattan views.
Hands-on science museum in a 1964 World's Fair pavilion, with 450+ interactive exhibits and a large outdoor Science Playground.
Film and TV history at the historic Kaufman Astoria Studios complex, with movie artifacts, a Jim Henson gallery, and daily screenings.
Riverfront park with restored 1920s rail gantries and the landmarked 1940 Pepsi-Cola neon sign, facing the Midtown skyline across the East River.

P.n: USTA Billie Jean King National Tennis Center
P.ad: Flushing Meadows Corona Park, Flushing, NY 11368
P.w: Year-round public tennis complex and home of the US Open since 1978, anchored by 23,000-seat Arthur Ashe Stadium.

P.ad: 175-10 Cross Bay Blvd, Broad Channel, NY 11693
P.w: A 9,000-acre National Park Service refuge of salt marsh and freshwater ponds, one of the Northeast's premier urban birding sites on the Atlantic Flyway.

P.n: Hindu Temple Society of North America (Ganesh Temple)
P.w: The first traditional Hindu temple in North America, built in 1977 of granite imported from India, dedicated to Lord Ganesha.
The nation's first and largest garden-apartment community, built 1914-1939 in Tudor and Mediterranean revival styles around hidden interior gardens.
A 39-acre garden with rose, herb and bee gardens and an award-winning LEED Platinum visitor center, at the edge of Flushing's Chinatown.
The largest metropolitan zoo in the US, 265 acres with 6,000+ animals, run by the Wildlife Conservation Society since 1899.
A 250-acre National Historic Landmark garden with the Victorian-era Enid A. Haupt Conservatory and 50 acres of old-growth forest.
Home of the New York Yankees since 2009, in the Concourse neighborhood; hosts baseball plus NYCFC soccer and concerts.
A 28-acre public garden and cultural center in Riverdale on a bluff above the Hudson with sweeping Palisades views.
The 1812 farmhouse where Poe spent his last years and wrote 'Annabel Lee'; now a museum run by the Bronx County Historical Society.
A 400-acre National Historic Landmark garden cemetery, resting place of Duke Ellington, Herman Melville and Miles Davis.
A 1.5-mile island in Long Island Sound with a New England fishing-village feel, seafood shacks, marinas and yacht clubs.
The 'Boulevard of Dreams,' a 1909 Champs-Elysees-inspired axis lined with one of the nation's densest concentrations of Art Deco buildings.
A Greek Revival stone mansion (c.1836-42) in Pelham Bay Park with period rooms and a formal terraced garden.
The oldest surviving building in the Bronx, a 1748 Georgian fieldstone house in Van Cortlandt Park.

P.n: The Bronx Museum of the Arts
P.w: A free contemporary-art museum on the Grand Concourse focused on 20th- and 21st-century work by artists of African, Asian and Latin American descent.

P.n: Hall of Fame for Great Americans
P.w: The first US hall of fame, a 630-foot open-air colonnade (1901, Stanford White) on the Bronx Community College campus with 98 bronze busts.
A 1924 limestone Italian Renaissance mansion built as a retirement home for the formerly wealthy; now a community arts and events space.
The Bronx's only public beach, a mile-long crescent in Pelham Bay Park built as a WPA project under Robert Moses in the 1930s, nicknamed the 'Bronx Riviera'.

P.ad: 1 Bay Street, St. George Terminal, Staten Island, NY 10301
P.w: Free 25-minute harbor crossing between Whitehall (Manhattan) and St. George, passing within view of the Statue of Liberty; runs 24 hours, no ticket needed.
P.k: ferry, free, Statue of Liberty views

P.n: Snug Harbor Cultural Center & Botanical Garden
P.w: 83-acre campus of Greek Revival buildings, a Chinese Scholar's Garden, and botanical gardens on a former sailors' retirement home; grounds free dawn to dusk.
Living-history village and museum complex spanning 300 years of New York history, with restored houses and costumed interpreters; open Wednesday through Sunday afternoons.

P.ad: 210 New York Avenue, Fort Wadsworth, Staten Island, NY 10305
P.w: One of America's oldest military sites, guarding the Narrows beneath the Verrazzano bridge; the tiered granite Battery Weed and Fort Tompkins offer sweeping harbor views. Part of Gateway National Recreation Area.
Victorian Gothic cottage on the shore that was home to pioneering photographer Alice Austen; now a museum of historic and contemporary photography with Narrows views.

P.ad: North Shore Waterfront Esplanade, Bank Street, St. George, Staten Island, NY 10301
P.w: Two white sail-like forms framing the Manhattan skyline, honoring the 274 Staten Island residents lost in the September 11 attacks and 1993 bombing; each name inscribed on a granite plaque.
Gateway to the Staten Island Greenbelt, a 2,800-acre network of woodlands, wetlands, and marked hiking trails in the middle of the borough; center has exhibits and trail maps.

P.ad: 1000 Richmond Terrace, Building A, Staten Island, NY 10301
P.w: New York City's only remaining general-interest museum, covering art, natural science, and local history; located on the Snug Harbor campus in St. George.
17th-century stone manor near the southernmost point in New York State, where a failed 1776 peace conference between the British and American delegates was held during the Revolution.

P.n: Jacques Marchais Museum of Tibetan Art
P.w: Stone temple-style buildings and terraced gardens housing one of the largest collections of Himalayan and Tibetan art in the U.S.; the Dalai Lama visited in 1991.

P.ad: 200 The Promenade at Lighthouse Point, Staten Island, NY 10301
P.w: Museum on the grounds of the former U.S. Lighthouse Service depot beside the St. George ferry terminal, telling the history of American lighthouses and lightkeeping.
Compact West Brighton zoo known for its serpentarium and reptile collection, plus aquarium, big cats, and a children's farm; open daily with free Wednesday afternoons.
Wooded 90-acre preserve at the heart of the Greenbelt, laced with hiking trails, ponds, and boardwalks; a former Girl Scout camp turned nature sanctuary.
500-acre open-air sculpture park in the Hudson Highlands with monumental works by Calder, Serra, di Suvero, and a Maya Lin earthwork set across meadows and hills.
P.k: Hudson Valley (Orange County); ~1.5 hr drive, or Metro-North to Beacon plus shuttle. Seasonal (spring-fall), closed Tuesdays.

P.w: Dia's collection of 1960s-to-present minimal and land art in a former Nabisco box-printing factory, with vast daylit galleries of Richard Serra, Agnes Martin, and Dan Flavin.
P.k: Hudson Valley (Dutchess County); ~80 min on the Metro-North Hudson line to Beacon. Open Fri-Mon.

P.n: Walkway Over the Hudson State Historic Park
P.w: The world's longest elevated pedestrian bridge, a 1.28-mile former railroad span 212 feet above the Hudson linking Poughkeepsie and Highland.
P.k: Hudson Valley (Dutchess County); ~1.75 hr drive, or Metro-North to Poughkeepsie. Free; open daily 7am-sunset.

P.w: Six-story Rockefeller family mansion above the Hudson with Beaux-Arts gardens, a modern-sculpture collection, and a coach barn of classic cars and carriages.
P.k: Westchester (Sleepy Hollow); ~45 min drive. Guided tours only from the Philipsburg Manor visitor center. Tours are SUSPENDED for the 2026 season; confirm before visiting.

P.ad: 3006 Seven Lakes Drive, Bear Mountain, NY 10911
P.w: Hudson Highlands park with a summit auto road and Perkins Tower views toward the Manhattan skyline, a lakeside 1920s inn, a trailside zoo, and a merry-go-round.
P.k: Hudson Valley (Rockland/Orange counties); ~1 hr drive. Open year-round.

P.w: Well-preserved 19th-century riverfront village of antique shops and cafes across from Storm King, a gateway to Breakneck Ridge and Hudson Highlands hiking.
P.k: Hudson Valley (Putnam County); ~80 min on the Metro-North Hudson line, walkable straight from the station.

P.ad: 2107 New South Post Road, West Point, NY 10996
P.w: The nation's oldest continuously operating Army post and academy above the Hudson; public bus tours visit Trophy Point, the Cadet Chapel, and Battle Monument.
P.k: Hudson Valley (Orange County); ~1.5 hr drive. Access to the post is by guided bus tour only; bring government ID for the required background check.

P.w: Restored 18th-century Dutch-colonial milling and trading site with a working water mill, telling the story of the 23 enslaved Africans who ran it.
P.k: Westchester (Sleepy Hollow); ~45 min drive. Timed tours May-early November, Wed-Sun.

P.ad: 200 Morris Pesin Drive, Jersey City, NJ 07305
P.w: Waterfront NJ park facing the Statue of Liberty and Ellis Island, with the restored 1889 Central Railroad terminal, a 2-mile promenade, and ferries to the monuments.
P.k: New Jersey (Jersey City); ~25 min via PATH plus a short walk, or a quick drive. Open daily 6am-10pm.

P.w: 42-acre sculpture park and museum on former state fairgrounds, dotted with Seward Johnson's life-size bronzes set among gardens, ponds, and roaming peacocks.
P.k: New Jersey (Mercer County); ~1.5 hr drive, or NJ Transit to Hamilton. Closed Tuesdays.

P.w: Ivy League campus of Collegiate Gothic quadrangles anchored by 1756 Nassau Hall, once the U.S. capitol, with a free open-air Putnam sculpture collection.
P.k: New Jersey (Mercer County); ~1.5 hr by NJ Transit to Princeton Junction plus the Dinky shuttle. Free student-led campus tours.

P.w: Herzog & de Meuron-designed museum of American art in the Hamptons, strong in East End painters like Fairfield Porter and the region's postwar artists.
P.k: Long Island (Hamptons/Water Mill); ~2.5 hr drive, or LIRR to Southampton. Closed Tue-Wed.

P.ad: 71 Old Westbury Road, Old Westbury, NY 11568
P.w: Gold Coast estate of the Phipps family with a 1906 Charles II-style mansion and 200 acres of formal English gardens, ponds, and tree-lined allees.
P.k: Long Island (Nassau Gold Coast); ~45 min drive. Closed Tuesdays; grounds are seasonal, roughly April-December.

P.w: Robert Moses's 1929 Atlantic beach with 6.5 miles of sand, an Art Deco bathhouse and water tower, a long boardwalk, and a summer amphitheater.
P.k: Long Island (Nassau County); ~1 hr drive, or LIRR to Freeport/Wantagh plus a beach-bus shuttle. Busiest on summer weekends.

P.w: 168-foot black-and-white striped 1858 lighthouse on the barrier-island seashore, with a keepers' museum and a tower climb over the dunes and ocean.
P.k: Long Island (Fire Island); ~1.5 hr drive via the Robert Moses Causeway to Field 5, then a half-mile boardwalk. Seasonal; tower climbs weather-permitting.

P.w: New York's oldest lighthouse, authorized under George Washington and lit in 1796, at the easternmost tip of Long Island, with a museum and a tower climb.
P.k: Long Island (East End); ~3 hr drive or LIRR Montauk line, the farthest of these trips. Seasonal, roughly spring-fall.

P.w: Long Island wine-country estate near the Hamptons known for its dry rose and sparkling wines, with a year-round tasting room among the vines.
P.k: Long Island (East End/Sagaponack); ~2.5 hr drive, or LIRR to Bridgehampton plus a short ride. Tasting room open daily; reservations advised.

F.ad: 205 East Houston Street, New York, NY 10002
F.w: Cash-and-ticket Lower East Side deli open since 1888, serving 15,000 lbs of pastrami a week under old neon and salami-hanging signs.
Greenwich Village slice institution since 1975, turning out thin, foldable New York-style plain slices from a stand-up counter until the early hours.
Chinatown counter for Xi'an-style hand-pulled biang biang noodles and cumin lamb, grown from a Flushing basement stall into a beloved local chain.

F.ad: 179 East Houston Street, New York, NY 10002
F.w: Family-run appetizing shop since 1914, slicing smoked salmon, whitefish, and sable behind the counter of a landmark Lower East Side storefront.
Chelsea Market taco stand griddling adobada pork shaved from a trompo onto hand-pressed tortillas; standing-room only and near-constant lines.
1885 Garment District chophouse famous for its mammoth mutton chop, dry-aged steaks, and ceilings hung with thousands of clay churchwarden pipes.
Original Upper West Side basement bakery known for its thick, gooey-centered six-ounce chocolate chip walnut cookies baked to order.

F.ad: 328 Malcolm X Boulevard, New York, NY 10027
F.w: Harlem soul food landmark founded by Sylvia Woods in 1962, serving fried chicken, braised oxtails, and cornbread with weekend gospel brunch.
Cash-only Williamsburg institution since 1887; the broiled dry-aged porterhouse arrives sizzling in its jus.
Bushwick wood-fired pizzeria whose Bee Sting pie pairs tomato and mozzarella with soppressata and spicy honey.
Midwood pizza shrine since 1965; the classic round pie is finished with hand-torn basil and grated cheese.
Bensonhurst landmark since 1939 known for the upside-down Sicilian square slice and house-made spumoni.
The 1916 Coney Island original at Surf and Stillwell, home of the July 4 hot-dog eating contest.
Chef Rawia Bishara's Bay Ridge Palestinian restaurant since 1998; known for muhammara, fried cauliflower and knafeh.
Downtown Brooklyn diner since 1950 famous for its dense New York-style cheesecake.
Cavernous Sunset Park banquet hall with roving carts of dim sum; a MICHELIN Guide pick for har gow and rice rolls.
Perennially packed, no-reservations Astoria taverna considered among the city's best Greek seafood; expect a wait for the charred octopus.
Michelin-recommended Flushing institution famous for delicate, broth-filled Shanghai soup dumplings pleated to order.
The brick-and-mortar home of Maria Cano, the legendary Jackson Heights street vendor, serving sweet grilled corn arepas.
Fiery, regional Thai cooking in Elmhurst that draws citywide crowds for its panang duck, crispy pork and drunken noodles.
Tiny cash-only Flushing counter beloved for its No. 6, a dozen tender pork wontons swimming in roasted-chili oil.
Refined Chiapas-inspired Mexican in Long Island City, a former Michelin-starred spot known for cochinita pibil and mole de Piaxtla.
A hidden Tibetan counter tucked behind a cell-phone shop, an open secret for hand-pleated momos and thukpa noodle soup.
All-vegetarian South Indian canteen in the basement of the Ganesh Temple, prized for crisp dosas, idli and sambar at bargain prices.
Chef Roberto Paciullo's flagship trattoria off Arthur Avenue serving the country cooking of Salerno with handmade pasta and daily specials.
Family-run Mott Haven Oaxacan restaurant renowned for a rainbow of hand-ground moles, including the rare mole blanco.
A 1940s Italian deli counter inside the WPA-built Arthur Avenue Retail Market, known for house mozzarella and overstuffed heros.
Roberto Paciullo's Salernitano trattoria and pizzeria on Arthur Avenue, named for the area code of his hometown.
Cash-only Arthur Avenue institution since 1962 with communal tables, no menus and no reservations; servers recite the day's dishes.
Waterfront seafood house at the tip of City Island with outdoor seats on Long Island Sound, serving lobster and fried seafood since 1939.
Founded 1953 in Riverdale, the last kosher deli in the Bronx, famed for hand-carved, piled-high pastrami.
Neighborhood slice shop on the corner of Arthur Avenue since 1976, known for its Sicilian pan pizza and calzones.
Bib Gourmand trattoria near the St. George ferry where a rotating cast of grandmothers cook regional Italian and 'Nonnas of the World' menus that change nightly.

F.ad: 524 Port Richmond Avenue, Staten Island, NY 10302
F.w: Blue-collar Port Richmond tavern serving thin, crackly-crust pizza since 1937 under the motto 'In crust we trust'; the plain cheese and garlic-onion white pies are the classics.
Family pizzeria running since 1960, famous for a paper-thin cracker crust and its vodka-sauce pie topped with fresh mozzarella and basil.
Cash-only Dongan Hills neighborhood tavern open since 1940, prized for a thin-crust white clam pie and old-school bar-pizza atmosphere.
Elaborately decorated Stapleton restaurant, among the first Sri Lankan spots in NYC, known for its weekend all-you-can-eat buffet of curries served on banana leaves.
Tiny, cash-only Tompkinsville storefront in 'Little Sri Lanka' cooking homestyle rice-and-curry and string hoppers from a steam-table counter since the late 1990s.

F.ad: 501 Port Richmond Avenue, Staten Island, NY 10302
F.w: The original 1928 Port Richmond stand, a summer institution serving scores of Italian-ice flavors plus cream-ice and ice-cream combinations from a walk-up window.
Two-Michelin-star farm-to-table destination at the Stone Barns agriculture center, serving a long tasting menu built from the surrounding fields and livestock.
F.k: Westchester (Pocantico Hills); ~45 min drive. Reservation-only, prix fixe; among the country's hardest tables to book.

F.w: Waterfront lobster deck and seafood market on Fort Pond Bay, an order-at-the-counter Montauk institution famed for its lobster roll and sunset harbor views.
F.k: Long Island (Montauk); ~3 hr drive or LIRR Montauk line. Seasonal; casual outdoor picnic-table seating over the water.

F.w: Eric Ripert's Midtown seafood temple, holding 3 MICHELIN Stars and a fixture atop the global best lists.
West Village Tamil kitchen from chef Vijay Kumar, a 1 MICHELIN Star and NYC's only starred Indian restaurant.
Rich Torrisi's imaginative Italian-American room in the Puck Building, awarded 1 MICHELIN Star.
Stefano Secchi's Flatiron ode to Emilia-Romagna pasta, a 1 MICHELIN Star handmade-pasta destination.
JP and Ellia Park's 14-seat NoMad counter, holding 2 MICHELIN Stars for its New Korean tasting menu.
Unapologetically rustic regional Indian in Essex Market, a MICHELIN Bib Gourmand pick on the Lower East Side.
Wood-fired Mexican in Greenpoint with house blue-corn tortillas, awarded 1 MICHELIN Star.
Calvin Eng's retro Cantonese-American diner in Williamsburg, a MICHELIN Bib Gourmand for value cooking.
East Williamsburg Taiwanese-American favorite, a repeat MICHELIN Bib Gourmand for zha jiang mian and fried chicken.
Sunset Park Sichuan superstar with lines out the door, recognized as a MICHELIN Bib Gourmand.
Flushing crowd-pleaser spanning Shanghai and Sichuan regions, a MICHELIN Bib Gourmand original location.
Hidden Sichuan stalwart off Flushing's Main Street, a MICHELIN Bib Gourmand for its fiery, creative plates.
Whitestone destination for southwestern-China heat and smoke, a MICHELIN Bib Gourmand Sichuan kitchen.
Second-floor Tibetan comfort-food mainstay on Jackson Heights' 74th Street, a MICHELIN Bib Gourmand for its momos.
Washington Heights Singaporean spot, grown out of the Queens Night Market, ladling out a rich coconut curry laksa and chili crab uptown.
Michelin Bib Gourmand East Village Vietnamese from the Banh Shop House team; in-house baked banh mi and a soulful pho with homemade noodles.
Michelin Bib Gourmand Vietnamese just off Union Square, pouring a fragrant pho over thin slivers of Miyazaki A5 wagyu tableside.
No-frills Sunset Park counter turning out one of the city's best banh mi, layered with pate, ham, head cheese and pork roll for around ten dollars.
Regal cart-service dim sum palace in Flushing where crisp deep-fried shrimp rice rolls, taro puffs and caramelized chicken feet zoom past on weekend mornings.
One of the largest Manhattan Chinatown dim sum parlors still running push carts, delivering quality siu mai, chicken feet and pork buns since 1989.
Cash-only Chinatown takeout legend whose sweet, tender roast pork over cabbage and gravy-soaked rice starts around five dollars and draws a permanent line.
Cash-only Mott Street hole-in-the-wall with a giant duck statue out front, roasting mahogany-skinned Cantonese duck, crispy pork belly and char siu.
Michelin Bib Gourmand anchor of Elmhurst's Little Thailand serving fiery Isan northeastern cooking, from rich khao soi beef shank to Zaab Zaab wings.
East Village outpost of the Bangkok Isan specialist, built around bright, pounded som tum papaya salads and Laotian-influenced northeastern Thai plates.
Three-decade Elmhurst Malaysian institution, cash-only, reliably excellent for flaky roti canai, curry laksa, char kway teow and Hainanese chicken.
Warm, lodge-like Manhattan Chinatown Malaysian favorite known for tangy asam laksa, cold Hainanese chicken and okra with shrimp.
Rare Sumatra-focused Indonesian spot in Elmhurst near the LIRR tracks, praised for nasi campur rendang with tender, slow-spiced beef.
Halal Indonesian comfort-food kitchen in Elmhurst known for creamy peanut-dressed gado-gado, ketoprak and batagor.
Boundary-pushing East Village Filipino from chef Eric Valdez and the Unapologetic Foods team, spreading fried duck and lemongrass pork belly kamayan-style on banana leaves.
Home-style Filipino cornerstone of Woodside's Little Manila since 1992, famous for sizzling pig-head sisig and peanut-rich oxtail kare-kare.
Family-run Michelin-listed East Village Burmese spot, the city's standout for laphet thoke fermented tea leaf salad and coconut chicken noodle soup.
Chef Nasim Alikhan's modern Prospect Heights Persian dining room, celebrated for its shattering tahdig crust, kuku sabzi and sabzi polo with fish.
Stylish Bushwick Persian small-plates spot from ex-Sofreh chef Ali Saboor, plating fava bean borani, wagyu kebabs and crackling potato tahdig.
Sourdough bagels that blew up on TikTok, drawing weekend lines so long the East Village shop reportedly faced landlord eviction threats.
TikTok turned its burrata-and-vodka-sauce chicken cutlet hero and square Sicilian slices into a citywide, line-out-the-door obsession.
Queens taco truck that ignited NYC's quesabirria craze after a glowing NYT review and viral broth-dipping taco videos.
Rode the viral Dubai-chocolate wave, reportedly selling 100+ pistachio-and-kataifi bars a day as the treat took over social feeds.
Instagram-famous laminated-pastry bakery whose over-the-top cruffins and croissants draw hour-plus weekend lines on the LES.
Birthplace of the Cronut, the croissant-doughnut hybrid whose 2013 debut sparked the modern viral-pastry era and still sells out.
Brooklyn Heights bakery whose 'croissant cereal' went viral, drawing hours-long weekend lines for warm French pastries.
Chinatown shop that broke Instagram with pastel unicorn soft serve served in a griddled fish-shaped taiyaki cone.
Flushing stall that turned Cantonese cheung fun into a social-media hit with mesmerizing rice-roll prep videos and long lines.
East Village smashburger that went viral for its griddled cheese-crusted patties, fueling a rapid multi-city expansion.
Greenpoint bakery that sold out 600 pastries on opening day and keeps drawing hour-plus lines for viral croissants and focaccia.
